questions.q: What does it mean that InnoDB's primary key is "clustered," per this lesson?
options: The table's data rows are physically stored in primary key order inside the primary key's own B-tree
The primary key is stored on a different, dedicated server
Clustered means the table has no primary key at all
It means multiple tables share one physical primary key
questions.explain: InnoDB stores actual row data within the primary key's B-tree structure itself, rather than in a separate heap.

questions.q: Why does a secondary index lookup in InnoDB require an extra step, per this lesson?
options: A secondary index stores the primary key value, and finding a row means looking that primary key up in the clustered index
Secondary indexes are stored on a remote replica server
InnoDB does not support secondary indexes
Secondary indexes always return incorrect results without a rebuild
questions.explain: Because data lives in the clustered (primary key) index, a secondary index match still requires a lookup back into that clustered structure.

questions.q: Why does a randomly-ordered primary key (like a UUID) cause more fragmentation than a sequential one, per this lesson?
options: New rows must be inserted in the middle of the existing B-tree repeatedly, causing page splits
UUIDs are too long to be stored as primary keys
Random primary keys are rejected by InnoDB at insert time
UUIDs disable indexing on the table entirely
questions.explain: A sequential key appends to the end of the clustered B-tree; a random key forces mid-structure inserts, causing page splits and fragmentation.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which query does an index on (last_name, first_name) efficiently serve?
options: A query filtering on last_name alone, or on last_name and first_name together
A query filtering on first_name alone
Only a query that filters on neither column
Only queries with no WHERE clause
questions.explain: A composite index is usable only via a left-to-right prefix of its columns, so last_name alone (or with first_name) is served, but first_name alone is not.

questions.q: What happens if a table has no explicitly defined primary key in InnoDB, per this lesson?
options: InnoDB silently creates an internal hidden clustered key, which you cannot reference or control
The table cannot store any data
InnoDB automatically converts the table to MyISAM
All queries against the table return an error
questions.explain: InnoDB requires a clustered key concept for every table, and without an explicit one, it creates a hidden internal key you have no control over.
